question.prompt: Janet rolls a standard \(6\)-sided die \(4\) times and keeps a running total of the numbers she rolls. What is the probability that at some point her running total will equal \(3?\)

solutions.title: List the possible beginnings
solutions.explanation:
Every roll increases the running total, so Janet can reach \(3\) only once, and she must do so within the first three rolls. This lets us list all successful beginnings:

- On the first roll: \(3\).
- On the second roll: \(1,2\) or \(2,1\).
- On the third roll: \(1,1,1\).

These are exhaustive because they are all the ordered sequences of positive integers with sum \(3\). The fourth roll cannot first produce a total of \(3\), since four rolls total at least \(4\).

For a specified beginning of length \(r\), independence gives probability \((1/6)^r\). Any rolls after reaching \(3\) are unrestricted. Also, the four listed beginnings cannot occur together, so we add their probabilities:
\[
\frac16+\frac1{36}+\frac1{36}+\frac1{216}
=\frac{36+6+6+1}{216}
=\frac{49}{216}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\frac{49}{216}}\), choice \(\text{B}\).

solutions.title: Work with smaller targets
solutions.explanation:
After a roll below the target, the same problem remains with a smaller target. Because every roll adds at least \(1\), reaching any target of at most \(3\) takes at most three rolls, so four available rolls are enough.

For \(r=0,1,2,3\), let \(p_r\) be the probability that future rolls reach an additional total of exactly \(r\) before passing it. We have \(p_0=1\), since no additional points are needed.

For a positive target \(r\), a first roll of \(k\le r\) leaves target \(r-k\). That first roll has probability \(1/6\), and the later rolls are independent of it. A roll larger than \(r\) fails. Thus
\[
p_1=\frac{p_0}{6}=\frac16,
\]
\[
p_2=\frac{p_1+p_0}{6}
=\frac{1/6+1}{6}=\frac7{36},
\]
and
\[
p_3=\frac{p_2+p_1+p_0}{6}
=\frac{7/36+1/6+1}{6}
=\frac{49}{216}.
\]
Therefore the requested probability is \(\boxed{\frac{49}{216}}\), choice \(\text{B}\).
